title: Chris Mason: Lib Dems rally behind Davey after recent resignations
description: The Liberal Democrats don't tend to go for rhetorical fireworks or verbal kneecappings when grumbling about their leader.But that doesn't mean there h
body: The Liberal Democrats don't tend to go for rhetorical fireworks or verbal kneecappings when grumbling about their leader.But that doesn't mean there hasn't been grumbling going on. In the last week, two members of Sir Ed Davey's frontbench have resigned because they were unhappy with him, the party's direction and how policy is decided.It meant the prospect of a lengthy and potentially testy meeting for Sir Ed with his MPs on Tuesday evening.The Liberal Democrat leader arrived smiling, flanked by several loyal MPs, but made no comment as he entered the room.Nearly four hours later, when the meeting broke up, his deputy Daisy Cooper said: "There is overwhelming support for Ed in the parliamentary party and a real sense that we need to come together as a group."Earlier, behind closed doors, we understand Sir Ed told his MPs: "We have made changes. I am happy to embrace more changes. I want us to work as a united front." Another tacit nod to things being less than united recently.In recent months he has appointed a new chief of staff, Ruth Younger, and James Holt, a veteran of the party's years in coalition government, as political director.Last week's resignations were described to the BBC by one party figure as a rather Lib Dem insurrection – dissent expressed modestly. Neither Charlie Maynard, a former Treasury spokesman and Alison Bennett, a former care and carers spokeswoman, have been publicly explicit about the reasons for their departures and both sought to express their concerns to Sir Ed privately and discreetly. And, it is understood, there was no coordination between them in the timing of their resignations. They were departures that led to fury among some of their colleagues, irritated that it made the party look divided.The resignations were the most clear indicators yet of an anxiety that has been bubbling away for over a year among some Liberal Democrat MPs. The essence of that anxiety is a fear they are not making enough of an impression and impact for the 72 MPs they have in parliament."The big frustration is the lack of cut through, being noticed. We are the biggest third party in the Commons in a century. But parliament doesn't shape things as much as it used to. It's about algorithms now," is how one figure put it.They added: "In the world of social media there is an incentive, even a financial incentive, to be divisive and extreme. That's a sandpit we refuse to play in."Nonetheless, the party is planning to up its social media game, but do so in line with what it sees as its authentic temperament and values.Those around Sir Ed Davey privately acknowledge there is what they claim to be a "small group" of Lib Dem MPs who are not happy with his leadership. It is suggested that number isn't greater than "half a dozen" - a phrase used by several people we have spoken to. But the anxiety about a perceived lack of impact involves far more MPs than that.Some previous private critics have been won over by the recent changes to Sir Ed's team and are pleased to see the government talk about issues they care about: the European Union, changing the voting system for Westminster elections and social care in England, for instance.They also hope the scale of their local campaigning, rather than poor national opinion poll ratings, will be more significant come the next general election.Al Pinkerton, the party's Europe spokesman, told the BBC there had been a frank exchange of views during the meeting, but Sir Ed's willingness to make changes had been "very well received.""It is a slog in the middle of a parliament, it's hard being the third party and it's such an enormous leap going from 15 MPs to 72," another party figure present told us. "But we're getting there putting in place the structures to better deal with that and keep MPs happy.""Why would we get rid of our leader when no one else is pitching to be our leader? We need to let Ed get on with it," said another MP.But they all know the underlying concern about impact – the challenge of being noticed – is real and not going away.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Lib Dems rally behind Davey after recent resignations

title: Actress Selma Blair faces additional charges for assault after plane incident
description: US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a fl
body: US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight. Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board.While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment".Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail.She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner.Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane. One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse.

schema.headline: Actress Selma Blair faces additional charges for assault after plane incident

title: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate it
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia.Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth.Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia."My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe."It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do."Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth £1.6bn over the next four years.The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports.The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire.Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued.On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

schema.headline: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street

title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office
description: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. A
body: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customis[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

schema.headline: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office

title: Lena Dunham's Girls returning for limited run at HBO
description: HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writ
body: HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars –  shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells. All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer. "We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement."I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said. "Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said. Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting. It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s. The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century."We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said. "To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival. Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude."I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.

schema.headline: Lena Dunham's Girls returning for limited run at HBO

title: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case
description: "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short
body: "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added. Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals. In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims"."While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra. Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended. The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault. Cornell case highlights 'draining' maze for victims to report campus sex assaultsThe president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus. These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said. Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations. Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe. State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case. Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

schema.headline: Cornell cancels fraternity parties over sexual assault case

title: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
description: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medica
body: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma."The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room."The pontiff had a "peaceful night" in the hospital, the Vatican said on Wednesday morning, where he is expected to remain for about a week.The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".Earlier, large crowds waited for hours outside the hospital for the Pope.They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".A Vatican source told the AFP news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world."Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.Carla had come specially, wanting to be close."He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray.""I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff."It turns out he's vulnerable too," she added.Elise Ann Allen, who wrote a biography of the Pope, told the BBC it would be "premature to be alarmed, but it's also premature to say everything's fine". She urged against complacency, telling the World Service's Newsday programme: "We really have to wait and see what the doctors say in the coming days".Allen added: "We don't know how much of a crisis it is at this point, but it's certainly a scare." She suggested that the world would see "a more determined Pope after this".In the wake of the announcement of Pope Leo's diagnosis, it emerged that his brother, Louis Prevost, was also being treated for cancer of a different kind. Prevost was being treated in the US for multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, his wife told the BBC's partner CBS News. His wife did not say what stage Prevost's cancer had reached.

schema.headline: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says

title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
description: The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and
body: The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed. A reopening date has not been confirmed."William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time"."The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued."The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers.An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday.Footage of the incident has been widely shared on social media, including on Tuesday evening by US President Donald Trump.The incident, which took place shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday, led to the evacuation and ongoing closure of the park.An eyewitness described seeing Chapman wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in.Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.Chapman was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe."We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us," the school said in a tribute on Tuesday."It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.""Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time," the statement continued.As a child, Chapman appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd.He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories.Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park have separately said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" are with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to Chapman's family and those who were at the scene.

schema.headline: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack

title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
description: The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday."Of
body: The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday."Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday."Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident. The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground. "It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him. One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement. Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed". "Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was  yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen." He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched. Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears."I broke because we were just on there," she said.Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death. He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach."Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account."His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet. In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

schema.headline: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster

title: Villa Park: Is stadium rebuild affecting Aston Villa's performances?
description: Fenerbahce visit on Wednesday as Champions League football returns to Villa Park.With them is Marcos Asensio, who scored eight goals for Emery's men d
body: Fenerbahce visit on Wednesday as Champions League football returns to Villa Park.With them is Marcos Asensio, who scored eight goals for Emery's men during a successful loan from Paris St-Germain in 2025 - and a reminder of the swagger Villa used to have at home.He scored in Saturday's 3-0 win over Rizespor, with Fenerbahce netting 11 goals in their last two games, including an 8-0 victory against Turkish Super Lig strugglers Eyupspor. That could present a problem for a Villa defence that has kept just one clean sheet this season and been increasingly fallible at home, something Emery knows must improve regardless of the rebuild."Our handicap is less supporters for the situation, but the club decided it. It is something to improve us for the future," said the Spaniard."We must try to be together and without 7,000 supporters we must push everyone. We must play better football, compete better, be more focused. Those are more important than the stand."We are realistic with how we are working, improving. The things are not [good] enough yet, a lot of conversations with the team, meetings, video, practising and each match trying to show and improve."Villa, though, have lost just once at home in Europe under Emery - against Olympiacos in the Europa Conference League semi final in 2024 - and he ended their wait for silverware by lifting the Europa League in May."Over the last few years our home form has been amazing, especially in Europe," said defender Matty Cash. "We need to get back to that."I don't want to sound like I am making excuses, because obviously we have to deal with the circumstances and it is really good to make the stand bigger and the stadium bigger, but it is obviously different. "I am not going to sit here and lie and say it isn't but you have to deal with the circumstances. You can't make excuses. You have to play what is in front of you. When it is done it will be amazing but yeah, at the moment it is a bit different."Champions Arsenal and Forest have already claimed three points at Villa Park this season, with unbeaten Brentford taking a point.Nicolas Jackson's equalising goal against the Bees was the first Villa had scored in front of the skeleton that was their North Stand this season.Yet Villa's home struggles are not new. Since the turn of the year they have lost the aura of invincibility which Emery has brought since his arrival almost four years ago.Between November 2022 and January 2026, they lost just eight of 61 home Premier League games, winning 44 of them. That included 15 straight wins between March 2023 and December 2023. They also went 12 months unbeaten in the top flight between August 2024 and August 2025, but since the turn of the year Villa have been fragile at home in comparison.Defeats by Everton, Brentford, Chelsea and Tottenham threatened their top-four place last season, with Villa needing late goals to earn a draw against Leeds and claim victories against Brighton and Sunderland.That has continued this season with Villa Park's capacity down to around 37,000 in the void left by the North Stand, something Brentford boss Keith Andrews picked up on, saying he hated playing when one stand was missing. Villa could still make light of it in Europe, though, with Viking also travelling to Birmingham in the league phase on 21 October.After an opening win at Club Brugge, successive victories would put them on course for qualification before November, despite their home issues."It is a massive test against a good team but we need to be winning these games," added Cash. "That is the bar we have set for ourselves. Hopefully we can make it loud - three-stand loud."

schema.headline: Villa Park: Is stadium rebuild affecting Aston Villa's performances?

title: Women's World Cup play-offs: 'Unplayable' Georgia Stanway proves a 'warrior' for England
description: Stanway's strikes in the past five days mean she has netted 11 times in her last 11 matches for England.She also ranks inside the top three for most g
body: Stanway's strikes in the past five days mean she has netted 11 times in her last 11 matches for England.She also ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in international football since Euro 2025.While Wiegman was frustrated by her side's lack of ruthlessness in Greece, Stanway always looked dangerous and made sure she got on the scoresheet.It felt inevitable she would join in the fun in Leicester when Alessia Russo and Lauren James grabbed a double each.Stanway came close to matching them when the Arsenal midfielder coolly took control of a long ball inside the box with one deft touch and, with the second, fired it powerfully into the bottom corner.It would have been the perfect strike to mark an impressive few days, but it was ruled out for offside, much to Wiegman's dismay."She is always so eager to go towards goal. She has that tenacity in her," said the England boss when asked about Stanway's goalscoring form."She is always aggressive out of possession but also in possession. She scored a great header and controlled that really good ball from Alex Greenwood."That was really good athleticism and composure. Unfortunately that was disallowed, but it was really good!"Football is about scoring goals, but also playing in the pockets, keeping the ball and connecting with other players - and I was happy with her [doing those]."Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live that Stanway was "unplayable at times" against Greece on Tuesday night.She won all her tackles, had a 90% passing accuracy rate, took four shots, scored once and had another disallowed.It was also a slightly different role for Stanway for most of the match as she played more as a right winger after changes in the midfield."She has something different to others," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live."She is goal-orientated, has a great shot and the disallowed goal showed her great mobility and athleticism."When you really need a fight, or a duel, or a counter-attack breaking up, she is there. She is a warrior who you can play a possession game with too."Stanway was even more effective in a new-look midfield which included 20-year-old debutant Lexi Potter.Chelsea midfielder Potter provided cover that allowed the experienced Stanway and Keira Walsh to push higher up, while Lauren James played in the number 10 role.It proved to be an inspired change from Wiegman as Stanway caused problems throughout for the visitors and was able to adapt to the tweaks impressively."Stanway has shown how flexible she is, how exceptional she is both at the bottom end of the pitch, breaking up play, as well as at the top end," said Brown-Finnis. "She was playing as a second striker, playing out on the right, dropping deep as a number 10. She's been absolutely brilliant."England still have a job to do to qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil with a two-legged play-off tie against Ukraine to navigate at the end of the year.They have already beaten their opponents 9-1 on aggregate in two games of the league phase of the qualifiers.After Wiegman's formation experiment worked so well this week, could it be an option for the future that brings out the best in Stanway, as well as others?"I liked the balance of the midfield. There is a lot of competition going on in that area," said Wiegman."There were a few reasons. First of all, I wanted to see Lexi Potter deeper on the pitch and what that might bring. "There was also the option to put Georgia Stanway higher up the pitch. We wanted to score more goals and we know that she can do that."She can play in the pocket and also deeper on the pitch so we wanted to see all of that."

schema.headline: Women's World Cup play-offs: 'Unplayable' Georgia Stanway proves a 'warrior' for England

title: World's oldest shipwreck found off Kekova Island in Turkey
description: Figure caption, Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova IslandByAlison Francis, Rebecca Morelle and Kevin ChurchBBC News Scien
body: Figure caption, Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova IslandByAlison Francis, Rebecca Morelle and Kevin ChurchBBC News ScienceThe world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea."The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope,  just 30m beneath the waves.Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, differerent styles are linked to particular periods.The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old."Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research shipImage source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conservedDivers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue."I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae."It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said."It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefactsTravelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaelogy Association specialises in finding and studying them.Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel."We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years."We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring itThe Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.The oldest known shipwreck where some of the wood is still preserved was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

schema.headline: World's oldest shipwreck found off Kekova Island in Turkey

title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
description: Figure caption, Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?ByDaniel Thomas and Oliver SmithBusiness reportersUpda
body: Figure caption, Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?ByDaniel Thomas and Oliver SmithBusiness reportersUpdated 41 minutes agoWould you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI."Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicantsWhile Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates."That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."'More competition for students'This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process".According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. 'It's not a level playing field'Image source, EDFImage caption, EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employeesHollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process."What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates.But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews."A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says. And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI to screen candidates, more than half plan to introduce it due to the large volumes of applications they are receiving. Hollie Moody says EDF does not currently use AI screening but may have to in future. For her, the use of AI in job applications remains a "moral dilemma" that employers and candidates will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits."It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."Get in touchHave you used AI to apply for a job or are you an employer who uses AI to find the best candidate? Share your experiences

schema.headline: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire

title: Arsenal 3-0 Lille: Bukayo Saka responds to challenge as fringe players have mixed night
description: Bukayo Saka responded to the challenge set by Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as he proved a game-changer in the 3-0 Champions League win over Lille.The
body: Bukayo Saka responded to the challenge set by Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as he proved a game-changer in the 3-0 Champions League win over Lille.The England forward has been told he should aim to score "two or three" goals per game - such is his quality and the expectation from his boss.Saka did not achieve that tally against the French visitors, but he shook off illness to come off the bench and assist Eberechi Eze's strike that made it 2-0 before rolling in his side's third goal.The 25-year-old has now scored four goals in nine games this season and looks to be taking the next step in his evolution as Arsenal's key man.With the majority of his side's attacking play involving him, Saka has always been an influential figure.But with opposition defenders doubling up on him and injury issues over the past two seasons, there were doubts over whether Saka could still do what was asked of him in attack or if he had lost a yard of pace.Arteta has tweaked Saka's positioning this season and, prior to Lille's visit, said it has been done deliberately to get him closer to the goal."That is where we need to get him," said the Gunners boss before the Lille game. "And if he misses the chance, so be it. At the end, the more volume we generate, the bigger the probability of him scoring more goals."Saka's strike against Lille was a confident one-touch finish and came after he missed a late one-on-one opportunity in Saturday's Premier League victory over Leeds."He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins," said Arteta."That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well - he could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know."When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals."Saka has reached 20 goals in a season just once in his career for Arsenal, which came in the 2023-24 campaign and included 16 in the Premier League.But the winger has also been in good goalscoring form for England with five in his latest four matches, netting a double in the 7-0 Nations League demolition of Croatia in the recent round of internationals.Saka is now on 19 goals in major European competitions for Arsenal, only behind Thierry Henry (42), while he has nine assists in the Champions League which puts him behind Henry (16) and Cesc Fabregas (14).He has refused to disclose the targets he has set himself, but Arteta welcomed Saka's response following his message to do more in front of goal.The Spaniard said: "I don't know if that's the case, but I am very happy."He wasn't feeling that good yesterday and today, as he had some sort of illness. He wasn't ready to start but he was really wanting to contribute to the team if it was needed and he came on and made a huge impact and delivered with real quality."Arteta revealed he also spoke to Saka after telling the media about his desire for the player to have a greater impact."After the press conference... I said 'Bukayo, I just killed you in the press conference, good luck tomorrow'."He was laughing. He knows that we have discussed these kind of things and he takes it because he wants to be the best version of himself."In order to do that, you have to put big objectives and challenges and try to reason by working and being consistent - and when it doesn't work, keep going because he has the ability to do it."Arteta made five changes to the team that started the win over Leeds as the Gunners look to navigate six matches in all competitions during this month.Noni Madueke moved to the right wing after putting in a good performance on the left at the weekend, with Mikel Merino, Eze and Viktor Gyokeres all coming into the starting XI.Eze had started just two games in all competitions before the match with Lille and Arteta had said his attitude had been "phenomenal" despite a lack of game time.The 28-year-old showed flashes of his undoubted quality and his finish for Arsenal's second goal - and his first of the season - will give him confidence going forward.Madueke had a mixed night as he showed his ability to beat a defender, but questions remain over his end product - even if he provided the assist for Jurrien Timber's classy opening goal.However, it was not a good night for Gyokeres.The Sweden striker scored 21 goals overall last season as Arsenal won the title for the first time in 22 years and displayed his willingness to run and work hard.But Gyokeres had just 12 touches before being replaced, and Kai Havertz, as he so often does, looked a much better and more natural fit for the Arsenal frontline, teeing up Saka's goal too.Arteta brought on Saka, Havertz and Martin Odegaard after going 1-0 up and all three contributed to show why they are still the first names on the teamsheet and why the Arsenal boss will be so reliant on them if they are to achieve more honours.

schema.headline: Arsenal 3-0 Lille: Bukayo Saka responds to challenge as fringe players have mixed night

title: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away
description: Image source, Emma MooreImage caption, Emma Moore says the garden has given her family, including elder daughter Penelope, a focus following the death
body: Image source, Emma MooreImage caption, Emma Moore says the garden has given her family, including elder daughter Penelope, a focus following the death of baby MabelByGeorge SandemanUpdated 2 hours agoWhen Emma Moore's daughter Mabel died, visiting her in a cemetery felt too far away."I don't like going to them and I feel like [visits] fizzle out," she says. "At first, you'll go regularly and then it'll start being once a year."Mabel was born prematurely at 27 weeks in April, her lungs had not fully developed and she lived for just two days. Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet but she wanted a special place to feel close to her."So we created something in the garden... [to] always be reminded of her every day," she tells Morning Live. The stillness of green spaces "can help us connect with memories" of loved ones, says Andy Langford, clinical director at Cruse Bereavement Support.And there are ways to create a special place of calm to remember anyone you've lost - even if you don't have a garden or know much about plants.Image source, Emma MooreImage caption, Emma, with her partner Louis and daughter Penelope, says the garden reminds them of Mabel each day"I'd never done anything like this before, so I had no clue about where to start," says Emma, 35, who lives near Bolton with her partner Louis and daughter Penelope.She chose to dedicate a part of the garden with a willow tree to Mabel. "I've enjoyed doing the gardening and planting. It was nice to focus on something."Of all the flowers the family have planted in Mabel's garden, Emma's favourite are the lilies.Morning Live - Memorial GardensFamilies speak about the healing power of nature and how some have created dedicated green spaces at home.The story about memorial gardens starts at 1:02:20White lilies are said to represent peace and are a traditional choice for acts of remembrance in the UK, says botanist James Wong of BBC Gardeners' Question Time.The flowers are low maintenance and can last for decades, he says.The colour of flowers in your garden a personal choice, adds Wong.Some may find soft pink, mauve and lilac relaxing, while others may find yellows and reds more vibrant and lift the mood.Image source, Morning LiveImage caption, Emma hadn't done much gardening before but has enjoyed creating one for MabelWong says smell helps us connect to nature and works with the sight of beautiful flowers to create a peaceful atmosphere.Many rose varieties have a fragrance but Wong also suggests choosing plants with scented leaves for when flowers are not in bloom."If you were to plant something like a mint, a eucalyptus or a rose geranium - they have very strongly scented leaves and they're around for a long period of time."He also suggests evergreen Italian cypresses, tall and thin plants more commonly used for commemoration in warmer climates, as they are capable of growing "perfectly well outdoors in the UK". They have a woody aroma likened to pine or juniper.Wong also says chrysanthemums - "a classic funeral flower" in East Asian cultures - will also readily grow here. They have a herbal almost medicinal fragrance.Image source, Morning LiveImage caption, The family dedicated a part of their garden under a willow tree to MabelEmma has placed a bench with a plaque featuring Mabel's name near the willow tree. She often sits on the bench in the morning with a cup of tea."It's her little garden," says Emma. "It's a really personal space." Langford says benches are common in public memorial gardens because they offer "a sense of permanence" and, on a practical level, help you take a break from the stresses and rigours of everyday life.If you want to use plants to create a memorial space indoors on a balcony or window box, think about nearby seating for two which opens up the opportunity for conversation about your loved one.Image source, Emma MooreImage caption, Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet in her homeIf you don't have a garden, Wong suggests choosing commemorative house plants suited to warmer conditions.The peace lily, native to the rainforests of Colombia, will "grow perfectly well indoors all year round" but should be kept in warm conditions with low levels of light.Frangipanis are "incredibly popular [in] Southeast Asia" and grow well indoors provided they have a reasonable amount of space and are placed in bright, warm spaces all year.In Mabel's memorial garden there is also a swing surrounded by planters full of flowers. It's a place that has given Emma comfort. "I feel like I'm still very much grieving but I can just go and sit there and think about her and reflect on things."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away
